description: Using data analysis and Web development to explain trends in our Planets System.
summary:
Earth Trend Detective is a free web app that lets anyone investigate whether a place on Earth is really changing. Users click the globe or enter coordinates, choose one of 19 variables (heat, water, snow, sun or wind), and the app analyzes up to 45 years of NASA data (1981-2025). It reports how much a variable changed per decade and whether the change is statistically significant, in plain language. It combines linear regression with an AR(1) correction, the Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope, and labels each result “Significant,” “Suggestive” or “Not yet significant.”

NASA publishes decades of open data, but using it usually requires code and statistics skills. Our app removes that barrier, with nothing to install. It also helps people tell a real trend from noise, since one hot year or one storm proves nothing.
details:
What it does and how it works
Earth Trend Detective lets anyone investigate whether a place on Earth is really changing. You click the globe or type a latitude and longitude, pick one of 19 variables (heat, water, snow, sun or wind), and choose a period. The app pulls up to 45 years of NASA data (1981–2025) and runs the statistics for you. It then gives a plain-language verdict: how much changed per decade, and whether the change is statistically significant. It uses three methods: linear regression with an AR(1) correction, the Mann-Kendall test, and Sen’s slope. The verdict is “Significant” (p < 0.05), “Suggestive” (0.05 to 0.10) or “Not yet significant” (p > 0.10).

Benefits
NASA publishes decades of open data, but using it normally requires code and statistics skills. Our app needs no installation and no coding. Students and curious people can get a rigorous answer in seconds.

Intended impact
We want to help people tell real climate change from noise. One hot year or one storm proves nothing, so the app shows what is changing, by how much, and how certain we can be. We never say “there is no trend”, only “not yet significant”.

Tools and data

  • Data: NASA POWER (Langley Research Center) and NASA GIBS (ESDIS)
  • Statistics validated against SciPy and pymannkendall
  • Languages, frameworks and libraries: [e.g. JavaScript/React, Python, your globe library]
  • Hosting: Vercel
  • Hardware: [e.g. laptops]

Creativity
We turned statistics into a detective investigation: five steps, a globe to explore, and honest verdicts instead of just numbers. The app is also upfront about its limits: the data is ~50 km reanalysis, so it’s less certain in mountains and coasts. A straight-line fit doesn’t prove linearity, and “significant” doesn’t always mean “important”.

Factors we considered

  • Years in a row aren’t independent, so we corrected for that with AR(1).
  • Using three methods gives a cross-check instead of relying on one.
  • Plain language, so non-experts can understand the results.
  • Honesty about uncertainty and limits.
